title: About the project
text:
Project overview
RESA Project no. 115, Economic Viability of Rural Settlements in the Three Biomes of Mato Grosso: An Integrated Analysis of Sustainability, Carbon and Territorial Dynamics, is implemented by Mato Grosso State University (UNEMAT) with support from Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS) under Grant D-25-02928.
The central research question is whether rural settlements in Mato Grosso can be economically viable while keeping the forest standing. To answer it, the project takes an integrated view of territory, production, income and carbon. The planned end product is a Technology Package of tools, methods, models and recommendations for public policy.

The territory and geospatial technologies workstream covers geodesy, territorial and landscape analysis, secondary data, processing and the database. The socioeconomics and bioeconomy workstream covers field data collection, socioeconomic and bioeconomic analysis, valuation, scenario modelling, engagement, dissemination and database architecture. The carbon and environment workstream covers the carbon balance, environmental sustainability, forest ecology, biomass and carbon stocks, as well as scenario building and technical recommendations. These three workstreams, defined in the project proposal, contribute to the Technology Package.

Specific objectives
Table 2 sets out the project’s six specific objectives (SOs), with the theme and a description of each.



Table 2 – Specific objectives of the RESA Project





Objective
Theme
Description




SO1
Territory and land use
Map land use, land cover and the landscape in the pilot areas using remote sensing.


SO2
Production and income
Build a database on production, costs, profitability and income in family production systems.


SO3
Environment and carbon
Measure socio-environmental impacts and estimate the carbon balance (emissions and removals), also covering water and soil.


SO4
Bioeconomic scenarios
Simulate low-carbon scenarios using net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR) and payback, with carbon and payment for environmental services included.


SO5
Innovation and social capital
Analyse innovation capacity, knowledge diffusion and social capital in the pilot areas.


SO6
Technology Package
Integrate the results into a package of validated tools, methods, models and recommendations.

title: About the project
text:
Implementation phases
The project runs in three phases. Phase 1, assessment and evidence generation (SO1, SO2 and SO3), gathers information on territory, production, income and carbon from secondary and field data. Phase 2, strategies and viability modelling (SO4), builds low-carbon scenarios and carries out the financial analysis. Phase 3, Technology Package and engagement for implementation (SO5 and SO6), holds workshops with the settled families, consolidates the package and prepares a proposal for scaling up.

title: About the project
text:
Research scope
The spatial scope of the research is the 141 municipalities of Mato Grosso covered by the 2017 Agricultural Census. They form the state-wide baseline and are analysed using public secondary data. The three biomes provide the basis for comparison, with each municipality assigned to the biome that occupies the largest part of its area. The assignment uses the 1:250,000 map (2019) from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) and places 76 municipalities in the Amazon, 61 in the Cerrado and 4 in the Pantanal.
The field study has three pilot areas, one per biome: Vale do Arinos (Juara); Quatá and N. Sra. Aparecida (Lucas do Rio Verde); and Lambari (Poconé). They are described in Pilot areas. However, a municipality is not the same as a pilot area: municipal indicators provide context for the pilot areas but do not measure them.

title: About the project
text:
Website development
The website is built with Quarto and R. The data are prepared in Python from the project databases, which were frozen on 19 October 2026. The figures come from public sources and from the project’s own results, such as the Manuscript 1 typology. The public sources are IBGE, the National Institute for Colonisation and Agrarian Reform (INCRA), Observatório do Clima’s Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Removals Estimation System (SEEG) and the National Institute for Space Research (INPE). Each figure is shown with its source, unit and year, and Data gives details of sources and licences.
This is a preliminary version for the project team. It will be published on GitHub Pages once the project coordination team has approved it. All pages ask search engines not to index them, and the website has no sitemap for search engines.
The website has an English version, available via the flags in the menu bar. It is a translation of the Portuguese original and is still being reviewed by the team. If the versions differ, the Portuguese text prevails.

title: About the project
text:
Content rules
The website follows a set of content rules. The IBGE symbols X (suppressed), – (true zero) and … (not available) appear as published, and none of them is converted to zero or to an empty cell. Tables and files therefore show the symbol itself in the cell, and in files the sinal_<variable> column repeats it. On the map, X is shown in grey. For tenure, the 2017 Census category is always referred to as “grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title (2017 Census)”. This category is not equivalent to the total number of agrarian-reform settlers.
For the typology, the website uses only the municipal typology from Manuscript 1 (k = 5), and the type names remain provisional labels until the authors approve them. Throughout the website, the dominant biome is taken from the IBGE 1:250,000 map (2019). For deforestation, the only series used is the official one from PRODES, INPE’s satellite-based deforestation monitoring system. The series is available on TerraBrasilis and is shown with the correction note. The pilot areas appear with identifying details only, because the figures for families and area will be added once the sources have been reconciled.
The following are not published on the website: personal data of producers and beneficiaries (names, CPF/CNPJ and property-level environmental registry data), photographs of people, commercial databases with restricted licences, the full texts of manuscripts and articles, the budget, field data, photographs, and data from drones and LiDAR. For the project team, only names, roles and workstreams are published. For the literature, only metadata (authors, year, title, journal and DOI) and search counts are published, with no third-party abstracts.

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
text:
Context and objective
The Agricultural Census, conducted by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), asks producers about their land tenure status. One possible answer is grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title (2017 Census), coded as category 46504 in the IBGE Automatic Retrieval System (SIDRA). The category therefore records a declared tenure status. The Census does not ask whether an establishment is part of agrarian reform, and producers who have already received their title may declare themselves owners. Drawing on results from Manuscript 1, this page examines how far the category captures agrarian reform in Mato Grosso (MT).

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
text:
Data and sources
The analysis compares three sets of records. The first covers establishments in the census category, as published by IBGE, both for family farms and for all establishments (family and non-family farms). The second covers agrarian-reform establishments identified in the Census by IBGE jointly with the National Institute for Colonisation and Agrarian Reform (INCRA), using multiple criteria. The third comes from INCRA’s administrative records: the projects in the Agrarian Reform Projects Information System (SIPRA) and the list of beneficiaries from INCRA’s Regional Superintendency in Mato Grosso. The cards below show the size of each set of records in the state.

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
section: Coverage of agrarian reform by the category
text:
Coverage of agrarian reform by the category
Figure 1 summarises the main result of the comparison: category 46504 captures at most 26.8% of the agrarian-reform establishments identified in the Census.



Figure 1 – Agrarian-reform establishments identified in the Census: upper limit inside the census category and lower limit outside it




At most 11,248 (26.8%) in category 46504at least 30,766 (73.2%) outside it42,014 agrarian-reform establishments identified in the 2017 Census by IBGE and INCRA (Marques, 2021)






Even if all 11,248 establishments in category 46504 were agrarian-reform establishments, they would account for only 26.8% of the 42,014 that IBGE and INCRA identified in the 2017 Census. At least 30,766 (73.2%) therefore lie outside the category.

In family farming, the category’s coverage of INCRA beneficiaries in Mato Grosso is 0.116: 8,834 establishments against 76,247 beneficiaries. Many titled beneficiaries declare themselves owners: the owners of 10,479 family farms obtained their land through agrarian-reform titling or licence (2017 Census, table 6774). Added to category 46504, these establishments form the combined measure, which covers 23.66% of family farms.


Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), note to Table A.15; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census; INCRA, list of agrarian-reform beneficiaries in Mato Grosso (Regional Superintendency SR-13; settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017), used only for aggregate counts by municipality, with no personal data; Marques (2021). Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.

section: Census and INCRA compared by municipality
text:
Census and INCRA compared by municipality



Figure 2 – Census category and INCRA beneficiaries, by municipality









Reproduced from Figure 6 of Manuscript 1: (a) family farms in category 46504 per 100 family farms (2017 Census); (b) INCRA beneficiaries (settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017) per 100 family farms, allocated to municipalities by the area of the project polygons. The classes are the same in the two maps.


Source: calculations by the authors of Manuscript 1 based on IBGE, 2017 Agricultural Census; INCRA/SIPRA, Report 0227; INCRA, list of agrarian-reform beneficiaries in Mato Grosso (Regional Superintendency SR-13; settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017), used only for aggregate counts by municipality, with no personal data. Note: the types in the figure (T1 to T5) are the same as in the table and carry the same provisional labels.








Figure 2 shows that the spatial patterns of the two maps diverge: where INCRA records many beneficiaries, the Census often records few establishments in the category. In all, 41 municipalities have 50 or more beneficiaries per 100 family farms and less than 5% of family farms in the category: 29 in T1, 1 in T2, 10 in T3 and 1 in T5. The opposite pattern, with the category at or above the Mato Grosso mean and fewer than 10 beneficiaries per 100 family farms, occurs in 1 municipality (Tesouro).

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
text:
External validation
If the category measured agrarian reform, municipalities with more INCRA beneficiaries should have more establishments in the category. However, Table 1 shows that the association is weak and loses significance once spatial autocorrelation (the similarity between neighbouring municipalities) is controlled for with Dutilleul’s modified t-test.



Table 1 – Correlation between tenure measures and INCRA beneficiaries








Note: Spearman’s ρ between each measure and INCRA beneficiaries per 100 family farms [95% bootstrap CI]; p-values corrected for spatial autocorrelation (Dutilleul). Combined measure: category 46504 plus owners titled through agrarian reform.


Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), Table A.15; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census; INCRA, list of agrarian-reform beneficiaries in Mato Grosso (Regional Superintendency SR-13; settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017), used only for aggregate counts by municipality, with no personal data. Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.





The combined measure (ρ = 0.497 across all municipalities) tracks INCRA records more closely than the category alone (ρ = 0.175). Table 2 sets out the validation indicators by type.



Table 2 – External validation indicators for the census category, by type (provisional labels)








Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), Table A.15; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census; INCRA/SIPRA, Report 0227; INCRA, list of agrarian-reform beneficiaries in Mato Grosso (Regional Superintendency SR-13; settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017), used only for aggregate counts by municipality, with no personal data, and allocated by the area of the project polygons. Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.





The results by type show distinct patterns. T3 accounts for 36.2% of INCRA beneficiaries in Mato Grosso, but the category’s coverage there is only 0.027. Its projects are also older: the mean year of creation is 1993.2, and 55.9% of families are in projects created up to 1995. The low prevalence of the category in T3 therefore refers to the status declared to the Census. T3 is not a type without agrarian reform. In T4, 44.0% of beneficiaries are already titled in SIPRA, the highest proportion of any type, and coverage rises to 0.453 once owners titled through agrarian reform are included. In T2, 32.8% of families are in state projects, while T5 has the fewest beneficiaries per family farm (58.4 per 100). Figure 3 shows these associations municipality by municipality.



Figure 3 – Tenure measures and INCRA beneficiaries, by municipality









Reproduced from Figure A5 of Manuscript 1. Each point is a municipality: (a) % of family farms in category 46504, (b) tenure factor score and (c) combined measure, each plotted against INCRA beneficiaries per 100 family farms (on a logarithmic scale that allows for zero, known as symlog).


Source: calculations by the authors of Manuscript 1 based on IBGE, 2017 Agricultural Census (tables 6878 and 6774); INCRA, list of agrarian-reform beneficiaries in Mato Grosso (Regional Superintendency SR-13; settlers and titled beneficiaries approved up to 30 September 2017), used only for aggregate counts by municipality, with no personal data. Note: the types in the figure (T1 to T5) are the same as in the table and carry the same provisional labels.

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
text:
Statistical suppression in the category
IBGE suppresses cells that could identify a respondent, marking them with the symbol X. In category 46504, X never appears for the number of establishments: 106 municipalities have a value and 35 have – (true zero). For area, by contrast, X appears in 52 municipalities, leaving 44,431 ha (11.2% of the category’s area in Mato Grosso) suppressed. For persons employed, X appears in 50 municipalities.
For this reason, the percentage of area in the category, by type, covers only municipalities without X (see the typology page for the table of type profiles, which reproduces Table 3 of the manuscript). This website never converts the symbol X to zero.
Juara, the host municipality of the Vale do Arinos settlement project (PA), is an example of agrarian reform outside the category. It appears with – (true zero) in category 46504, meaning that the Census recorded no family farms with this status, although the municipality has settlement projects in SIPRA.


Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), Table 1; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census; Juara: data from this observatory (2017 Census, table 6878; INCRA/SIPRA, 2025). Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.

title: Agricultural Census tenure data and agrarian reform
text:
Concluding remarks
The census category measures declared tenure status and captures only part of the agrarian-reform establishments identified in the Census. This is evident both in the state aggregate and in the comparisons by municipality and by type. The combined measure, which includes owners titled through agrarian reform, tracks INCRA records more closely than the category alone. The category’s association with these records is weak and loses significance when spatial autocorrelation is taken into account.
These results have limitations. Area and persons employed in the category are subject to statistical suppression, and the Census and SIPRA have different reference years. The census category should therefore be interpreted as a measure of declared tenure status, not of agrarian reform. Whenever agrarian reform is the subject of analysis, the category must be compared with administrative records.

title: 2006–2017 dynamics by municipal type
text:
Context and objective
The project’s Article C compared the 2006 and 2017 Agricultural Censuses, both conducted by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). This page recalculates those results using the five types from Manuscript 1 (provisional labels) and the dominant biome from the IBGE 1:250,000 map. The aim is to examine how the number, area and mean area of establishments changed in each group.

title: 2006–2017 dynamics by municipal type
text:
Data and methods
The figures refer to all agricultural establishments, not only family farms, in the 141 municipalities of Mato Grosso (MT). Intercensal changes are calculated from the municipal sum for each group. Differences between types and between biomes are assessed with the Kruskal-Wallis test on municipal percentage changes, with no correction for spatial autocorrelation. The municipal sum for the first Census does not reconcile with the state table, as detailed in the box below and in Table 7 in the appendix to this page.



The 2006 municipal sum does not reconcile with the state table

The sum across the 141 municipalities comes to 112,987 establishments and 48.69 million ha in 2006. The 2006–2017 state comparison table records 112,978 establishments and 47.81 million ha, a difference in area of 883 thousand ha (1.8%).
The IBGE Census comparison table (historical series) records 112,987 establishments and 48,688,710 ha in 2006, figures that match the municipal sum. It is not yet clear why these figures differ from the state table.
In 2017, the sum reconciles: 118,679 establishments and 54,922,849 ha, against 54,922,850 ha in the state total (a rounding difference).
The changes shown below use the municipal sum in both years, so that 2006 and 2017 share the same basis.





Value of production: excluded from this version






The 2006 value of production does not reconcile. The state table records R$9.60 billion, but the sum from the corrected municipal database (IBGE, table 1118) comes to R$12.29 billion, 28% more (2006 values at current prices). Until the difference is explained, the change in the value of production between 2006 and 2017 remains excluded from the website.

title: 2006–2017 dynamics by municipal type
text:
Concluding remarks
This page has recalculated the dynamics of agricultural establishments between the two Censuses using the five municipal types and the dominant biome. The sums indicate an increase in the number of establishments in T5, with mean area almost unchanged. They also indicate a decrease in that number in T4 and T3, with mean area rising in T4 and area rising in T3. The statistical evidence for these differences across municipalities, however, is not clear.
These results have limitations. The figures cover all agricultural establishments, not only family farms, and the municipal sum for the first Census does not reconcile with the state table. The value of production also remains excluded from this version until the difference is explained.

title: SO5 · Innovation and social capital
text:
Objective
The fifth specific objective (SO5) is to understand how families in the pilot areas innovate, exchange knowledge and organise themselves. SO5 seeks to identify the factors that favour engagement and how families perceive the proposed changes. This is expected to make the diffusion of the Technology Package more effective and to strengthen the network linking families, researchers and public authorities.




Status as at 19 October 2026: 
planned



planned
 
Participatory workshops in the pilot areas.
To be held after the Phase 1 assessment; no confirmed date.


planned
 
Workshop reports and community engagement protocols.


The badges are based on the project’s internal record and have yet to be validated by the project coordination team.

title: SO5 · Innovation and social capital
text:
Planned methods
The planned method combines participatory workshops with semi-structured interviews. The workshops with farmers and community leaders are intended to validate the results of the assessment and to develop the recommendations jointly. The interviews with families and community leaders aim to capture perceptions and engagement factors. Practical training in the pilot areas is also planned, covering low-carbon management and access to specialised markets, such as those for carbon credits and payment for environmental services (PES). Finally, a dissemination plan is to include field days and plain-language materials such as booklets, short videos and simplified maps.

title: SO5 · Innovation and social capital
text:
Expected results
The project proposal sets three targets for measuring progress on this objective. These are the degree to which communities engage with and take ownership of the Technology Package, the number of family farmers trained in low-carbon technologies, and the public policy proposals presented to decision-makers.

title: SO5 · Innovation and social capital
text:
Ethical considerations
Activities with families are subject to approval by the Research Ethics Committee and to the free and informed consent of participants. In keeping with these safeguards, the website does not publish the names, photographs or individual data of families or participants, and workshop results are presented in aggregate form only.


Source: compiled by the authors from the RESA Project proposal (specific objectives, methodology and dissemination plan).

title: SO3 · Environment and carbon
text:
Objective
The third specific objective (SO3) is to use indicators to measure the socio-environmental impacts of production systems in the pilot areas. It estimates the carbon balance between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and removals, and assesses the condition of water and soil. The results will inform the environmental guidelines of the Technology Package, as well as mitigation and adaptation policies.
Methods. The proposal is to estimate carbon stocks in biomass and soil, together with the emissions and removals associated with land-use change and management. These estimates will yield the net carbon balance of each pilot area.

The Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Removals Estimation System (SEEG) puts gross emissions for Mato Grosso (MT) in 2024 at 231.2 MtCO2e (million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent). Source: authors’ calculations based on SEEG 13, Observatório do Clima, state emissions by sector (GWP-AR5), 1990–2024. Note: SEEG estimates land-use change from 1990 onwards.



Methodological caveats
Some caveats apply to these figures. First, they are estimates: SEEG calculates emissions using its own methods and factors, and each new collection revises the entire series. The figures here are from collection 13. Second, these are gross emissions, so carbon removals by vegetation have not been deducted; municipal data on removals are in the climate indicators. Third, SEEG measures emissions across the whole territory of the state and its municipalities, not those of family farming or settlements.
The municipal sum does not match the state total. In 2024, the municipalities add up to 230.98 MtCO2e, against 231.17 MtCO2e for the state. The difference is the share of emissions that SEEG does not attribute to any municipality. Land-use change tracks deforestation but is not equivalent to it; the official deforestation series is in SO1. Finally, municipal SEEG data are shown on the website but left out of the downloads until the licence has been checked.

Objective
The first specific objective (SO1) is to produce a territorial and ecological assessment of the pilot areas using geospatial technologies. It maps changes in land use and land cover over time and measures landscape structure in terms of attributes such as the fragmentation and connectivity of native vegetation. This gives the Technology Package its technical and visual basis for discussions with families and public authorities about keeping the forest standing.
Analysis period. The proposal specifies the period from 1980 to 2023. However, the source of land use and land cover data planned for SO1 (MapBiomas, public data) has not yet been incorporated into this version. The period ultimately covered will depend on which collection is used.

section: Deforestation in Mato Grosso: the official PRODES series
text:
Deforestation in Mato Grosso: the official PRODES series



Correction note (19 October 2026). 
In the PRODES series previously used in project materials, the Amazon values had been entered by hand and were higher than the official Mato Grosso rate from 2005 to 2024. 
The website now uses only the official series from the National Institute for Space Research (INPE), available on the TerraBrasilis platform and retrieved on 19 October 2026. This series covers the annual rate for Mato Grosso in the Legal Amazon and the annual increment by biome.



The annual deforestation rate for Mato Grosso (MT) comes from PRODES Legal Amazon, the programme run by the National Institute for Space Research (INPE) that measures clear-cutting of forest formations. In 2025, the latest year with a consolidated rate, deforestation reached 1,593 km², a figure covering August 2024 to July 2025. The 2026 figure (849 km²) is still an estimate and is therefore not included in the chart below.


02 k4 k6 k8 k10 k12 k19901995200020052010201520202025Annual rate for MT (Legal Amazon)


As well as the rate, PRODES measures the deforestation increment in each biome, using a mask and method specific to that biome. The increment by biome is therefore not directly comparable with the Legal Amazon rate. The chart below shows annual periods only. PRODES publishes data for periods of two years or more in the Cerrado up to 2012 and in the Pantanal in some years up to 2016, and these have been excluded.

title: SO1 · Territory and land use
text:
PRODES deforestation by municipality (2017–2025)
PRODES also publishes the deforestation increment for each municipality, broken down by biome. In Mato Grosso, between 2017 and 2025 (PRODES years, covering August 2016 to July 2025), the programme mapped 14,869 km² in the Amazon, 6,777 km² in the Cerrado and 1,323 km² in the Pantanal. Over these nine years, the data for all three biomes are annual and consolidated.
The municipalities with the most deforestation over the period were Colniza (1,916 km²), Aripuanã (1,025 km²) and Marcelândia (837 km²). In the pilot-area host municipalities, the totals were 567.4 km² in Juara, 15.5 km² in Lucas do Rio Verde and 319.4 km² in Poconé. These figures refer to the entire municipal territory, not to the pilot areas.

Category 46504 of the 2017 Census (grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title) under-records agrarian reform, because producers who have already obtained their title appear as owners. SIPRA counts each settlement project only in its host municipality (INCRA, Report 0227, as at 3 June 2025). See Census tenure data and agrarian reform for a discussion.








SEEG estimates emissions for the whole municipality, not only for family farming (SEEG 13, Observatório do Clima, GWP-AR5).








The indicators under this theme cover all agricultural establishments (family and non-family farms). The 2006 municipal sum does not match the IBGE state table: 112,987 against 112,978 establishments and 48.69 against 47.81 million ha.

text:

The chart shows gross emissions and removals, along with emissions from land-use change and forestry and from agriculture and livestock, as estimated by SEEG 13 for the whole municipality from 1970 to 2024. Category 46504 of the 2017 Census (grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title) under-records agrarian reform, because producers who have already obtained their title appear as owners. text:
Preliminary version for the project team. Results may change as the study progresses.
 English translation under review. If the two versions differ, the Portuguese text prevails.
This page covers the 141 municipalities in the 2017 Agricultural Census. Boa Esperança do Norte was created later and is not included. Each municipality is assigned a dominant biome from the 1:250,000 biome map (2019) of the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). This places 76 municipalities in the Amazon, 61 in the Cerrado and 4 in the Pantanal. A municipality’s type is the group it belongs to in the municipal typology of family farming from RESA Project Manuscript 1 (M1). The type labels remain provisional until the authors approve them, and the profiles describe municipalities, not settlements.

title: AFS and PES in settlements
text:
The reference study
The study by Dominicis et al. (2023), published in Forests (10.3390/f14102110), assesses the financial viability of agroforestry systems (AFS) established by family farmers, most of them agrarian-reform settlers, in the Descoberto River basin (Federal District, Cerrado). The authors compare results with and without payment for environmental services (PES), using indicators such as net present value (NPV) and internal rate of return (IRR).
The specific objective on bioeconomic scenarios (SO4) will replicate and extend this design in the project’s three pilot areas, one in each biome. The search for similar studies serves a dual purpose: to inform the choice of methods and to show what is still missing from the literature.

title: AFS and PES in settlements
text:
Gaps in the literature
Comparing the studies points to five gaps in the literature. The project treats them differently, depending on the status assigned to each: three are confirmed, one is partly filled and one is not asserted. The first two, both confirmed, concern geographical coverage. The search found no viability study of AFS or productive restoration in a settlement in Mato Grosso (gap 1), and the studies conducted in the state deal with smallholdings outside settlements, commercial farms or experiments. Nor did it find any such study in the Pantanal (gap 2), so the closest parameters come from the Cerrado of Mato Grosso do Sul, in the transition zone with the Pantanal.
Gap 3, on valuing carbon at market prices in settlements and small-scale production, is partly filled. Some studies include carbon in the cash flow of small producers, although most were conducted outside Brazil; in Brazil itself, cases are few and partial. By contrast, gap 4, on treating PES, carbon, risk and differences between families together in the same study, is confirmed, as no study combines all four elements. This combination is therefore SO4’s contribution.
Finally, gap 5, on land credit debt in the cash flow, is not asserted. The search did not target this point, which is relevant to the N. Sra. Aparecida case (land credit). A dedicated search is therefore needed before this gap can be asserted.

Source: compiled by the authors from the RESA Project’s synthesis of the October 2026 search, set out in a separate text.

title: Data
text:
Files for download
All files are comma-separated and UTF-8 encoded, with a point as the decimal separator. Their headers and data dictionaries are in Portuguese. The id_municipio key is the 7-digit IBGE code, and each database has a data dictionary listing every column with its description, unit and source. In the Census databases, each variable has a sinal_<variable> column containing valor, X, – or …; where there is no number, the variable’s own column shows the symbol, as in the IBGE tables. In files that include the M1 type, the rotulo_status column indicates that the label is provisional.

title: Data
text:
Notes on the figures






NoteDiscrepancy between the municipal sum and the state total



The totals on the home page are the official state totals; the municipal sum gives slightly different values. For the area of establishments in 2017, the municipal sum is 54,922,849 ha, compared with a state total of 54,922,850 ha. For family farms, the corresponding figures are 5,131,101 ha and 5,131,104 ha. These differences are due to IBGE rounding (2017 Agricultural Census).
For gross emissions in 2024, the municipalities add up to 230.98 MtCO₂e, compared with 231.17 MtCO₂e for the state. The difference of about 0.19 MtCO₂e represents emissions that SEEG 13 does not allocate to municipalities.
In the 2006 Agricultural Census, the municipal sum gives 112,987 establishments and 48.69 million ha, compared with 112,978 establishments and 47.81 million ha in the 2006–2017 state comparison table. The difference in area is about 1.8%. The IBGE Census comparison table (historical series), by contrast, matches the municipal sum. For this reason, figures on the 2006–2017 dynamics always carry this note.








NoteTerms of use and attribution



Of the IBGE symbols, X indicates suppression: the value has been withheld so that the respondent cannot be identified. The symbol – indicates a true zero, and … indicates a value that is not available. In the files, the symbol appears in place of the number and is repeated in the symbol column. X and … do not mean zero. The symbol – does mean a true zero, but it is shown as –, not as 0. The application programming interface (API) of the IBGE Automatic Retrieval System (SIDRA) holds no irrigation record for Araguainha, so irrigation there is shown with the symbol … (value not available).
For tenure, category 46504 of the 2017 Census is “grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title (2017 Census)”. This category is not equivalent to the total number of agrarian-reform settlers. It should therefore be compared with data from the Agrarian Reform Projects Information System (SIPRA) of the National Institute for Colonisation and Agrarian Reform (INCRA). For the Manuscript 1 typology, the type labels remain provisional until the authors approve them, and anyone using them must cite the RESA Project.
Municipal data from SEEG 13 are shown on the pages, with their source, but are excluded from the downloads until the licence has been checked. They can be found at seeg.eco.br. For PRODES, the satellite-based deforestation monitoring system, the website uses only the official series from the National Institute for Space Research (INPE), published on TerraBrasilis and retrieved on 19 October 2026. The related correction note is on the Emissions and deforestation page. MapBiomas, planned for SO1, is not yet used in this version. For the literature, the files contain metadata only, with no third-party abstracts.

text:
Core readings
The six readings below guide the project’s socioeconomic strand. Each reference links to the publication at its original source.




Dominicis et al. (2023)
DOMINICIS, L. F. de et al. Payment for Environmental Services and the Financial Viability of Agroforestry Systems: an integrated analysis of socio-environmental projects in the Descoberto Basin—Federal District. Forests, v. 14, n. 10, 2110, 2023.

DOI 10.3390/f14102110

Reference study for SO4 (bioeconomic scenarios), analysing agroforestry systems (AFS) with and without payment for environmental services (PES) in settlements in the Federal District.


Silva et al. (2026)
SILVA, D. et al. Climate resilience through bioeconomy: a mixed-methods protocol for assessing adaptation policies in rural settlements on the Amazon. PLOS ONE, v. 21, n. 2, e0342911, 2026.

DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0342911

Mixed-methods protocol for settlements in the Amazon, used as a reference for the field instruments.


Cabral et al. (2026)
CABRAL, D. V.; SANTOS, L. F. dos; SIMONINO, C. T. Caracterização da agricultura familiar do estado de Minas Gerais por meio de seus fatores determinantes. Revista Econômica do Nordeste, v. 57, n. 3, e20262715, 2026.

Article page on the journal’s website
DOI to be confirmed

Factor-based characterisation of family farming in Minas Gerais using 2017 Census data. The project replicates the method and extends it to Mato Grosso. The printed DOI (10.61673/ren.2026.2715) is not yet registered with Crossref (checked on 19 October 2026).


Suela et al. (2026)
SUELA, A. G. L. et al. Avaliação do pagamento por serviços ambientais para incentivar a conservação da mata nativa no bioma Cerrado: uma análise de equilíbrio geral computável. Revista Econômica do Nordeste, v. 57, n. 4, e20262748, 2026.

DOI 10.61673/ren.2026.2748

PES value that offsets the returns from converting the legal reserve surplus in the Cerrado, used as an external reference for SO4.


Marques (2021)
MARQUES, V. P. M. de A. Estabelecimentos da reforma agrária no Censo Agropecuário 2017. Porto Alegre: INCRA, 2021.

Official INCRA page (PDF)

Identifies agrarian-reform establishments in the 2017 Census using a special tabulation produced by IBGE with INCRA. The study shows that the Census category does not cover the whole of agrarian reform.


IBGE (2019)
INSTITUTO BRASILEIRO DE GEOGRAFIA E ESTATÍSTICA (IBGE). Censo agropecuário 2017: resultados definitivos. Rio de Janeiro: IBGE, 2019.

IBGE Library (PDF)

Final results of the 2017 Census, including the categories of the producer’s land tenure status, such as grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title.





The DOIs for Dominicis et al. (2023), Silva et al. (2026) and Suela et al. (2026) were checked against Crossref. The page for Cabral et al. (2026) was checked on the journal’s website on 19 October 2026.

title: Carbon, markets and ESG
text:
Preliminary version for the project team. This page gives reference metadata only (authors, year, title, journal and DOI). A synthesis of the findings will follow in a future version, as a separate text.
 English translation under review. If the two versions differ, the Portuguese text prevails.
The literature review on carbon, markets and ESG (environmental, social and governance) is organised into six thematic blocks, each defined by a theme and a question. Its 115 references all have a digital object identifier (DOI) verified against Crossref (September 2026) and inform the specific objectives on environment and carbon (SO3) and bioeconomic scenarios (SO4). This page sets out the six blocks first, then the complete list of references, with files for download.

title: Carbon, markets and ESG
text:
Thematic blocks of the review





A · Foundations and design
14 references


Question: 
When does a tax dominate a cap? How do allocation, banking and stability reserves change prices and profits?




B · Ex-post effectiveness
19 references


Question: 
How much have markets and taxes reduced emissions? In which sectors? At what cost? Was there any emissions leakage, innovation or distributional effect?




C · Price econometrics
17 references


Question: 
What drives the price? Is it cointegrated with energy and commodity prices, and is there spillover between them? How should volatility and tails be modelled, and prices forecast?




D · Voluntary market
19 references


Question: 
Do REDD+ and other projects actually reduce emissions? What determines price and demand? Where do settlements come in?




E · Emissions in Brazil
22 references


Question: 
What explains municipal emissions trajectories? Is there convergence and spatial dependence? Which policies have reduced AFOLU emissions?




F · ESG and finance
24 references


Question: 
Are emissions and ESG priced in? Why do ratings diverge? How do investors react to climate risk?






Source: compiled by the authors from the RESA Project’s literature review (September 2026). To see a block’s references in the table of studies, select its card.

Category 46504 of the 2017 Census (grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title) under-records agrarian reform, because producers who have already obtained their title appear as owners. Category 46504 of the 2017 Census (grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title) under-records agrarian reform, because producers who have already obtained their title appear as owners. SIPRA counts each settlement project only in its host municipality (INCRA, Report 0227, as at 3 June 2025). See Census tenure data and agrarian reform for a discussion.








SEEG estimates emissions for the whole municipality, not only for family farming (SEEG 13, Observatório do Clima, GWP-AR5).








The indicators under this theme cover all agricultural establishments (family and non-family farms). The 2006 municipal sum does not match the IBGE state table: 112,987 against 112,978 establishments and 48.69 against 47.81 million ha.

Category 46504 of the 2017 Census (grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title) under-records agrarian reform, because producers who have already obtained their title appear as owners. SIPRA counts each settlement project only in its host municipality (INCRA, Report 0227, as at 3 June 2025). See Census tenure data and agrarian reform for a discussion.








SEEG estimates emissions for the whole municipality, not only for family farming (SEEG 13, Observatório do Clima, GWP-AR5).








The indicators under this theme cover all agricultural establishments (family and non-family farms). The 2006 municipal sum does not match the IBGE state table: 112,987 against 112,978 establishments and 48.69 against 47.81 million ha.

title: The project’s specific objectives
text:
Preliminary version for the project team. Results may change as the study progresses.
 English translation under review. If the two versions differ, the Portuguese text prevails.
The RESA Project aims to determine whether family farming in settlements across Mato Grosso’s three biomes can make the transition to a low-carbon economy that keeps the forest standing. The analysis integrates territorial, production, income and environmental dimensions to identify the factors that favour emission reductions, climate adaptation and long-term sustainability.
The project’s end product is a Technology Package: a set of tools, methods, models and recommendations designed to support public policy. The work is structured around three phases and six specific objectives (SOs). Phase 1, Assessment and evidence (SO1, SO2 and SO3), covers territory, production and income, carbon, water and soil in the pilot areas. Phase 2, Strategies and viability modelling (SO4), brings together low-carbon scenarios assessed with financial indicators. Phase 3, Technology Package and engagement (SO5 and SO6), includes workshops with families, consolidation of the package, training and public policy proposals.

title: SO4 · Bioeconomic scenarios
text:
Objective
The fourth specific objective (SO4) is to simulate viability scenarios for the low-carbon transition in the pilot areas. SO4 builds the value of carbon and environmental services into financial indicators in order to propose business models and public policy recommendations for the Technology Package.




Status as at 19 October 2026: 
in progress

The badges are based on the project’s internal record and have yet to be validated by the project coordination team.

title: SO4 · Bioeconomic scenarios
text:
Planned indicators and scenarios
The scenarios will compare a plot’s current use with low-carbon alternatives such as agroforestry systems (AFS) and integrated crop-livestock-forest systems (ICLF) on the same plot, with and without the project. The financial indicators for this comparison will be net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), the investment payback period and the benefit/cost ratio. Scenarios with and without payment for environmental services (PES) will also be considered, in order to identify the minimum payment that makes the transition viable.
Using publicly available prices, the project will estimate both carbon revenue and the carbon price at which the options being compared break even. Risk and sensitivity will be assessed by varying prices, productivity, losses and the discount rate, and by risk simulation. Finally, the scenarios will take account of the specific features of the pilot areas. In N. Sra. Aparecida, which falls under the National Land Credit Programme (PNCF), the instalments paid for the land will be included in each family’s cash flow.

title: SO4 · Bioeconomic scenarios
text:
Reference study
The scenario design uses the study below as its reference.




Dominicis et al. (2023), 
Forests
, 14(10), 2110. DOI 
10.3390/f14102110
.


The study assesses the financial viability of AFS run by producers, most of them from agrarian-reform settlements, in the Descoberto Basin, Federal District. 
The authors compare scenarios with and without PES, using indicators such as NPV and IRR.

SO4 will replicate the study’s design in the three pilot areas and add the elements missing from it: results per family, carbon and risk.

The sixth specific objective (SO6) is to bring together the project’s results and analyses in a wide-ranging database and a practical Technology Package of validated tools, methods, models and recommendations. The package is the project’s main instrument for dialogue with families and public officials, and for supporting policies that keep the forest standing at scale.

title: SO6 · Technology Package
text:
Planned methods
The planned method involves building a database and a system that bring together the assessment, strategies and models from the previous objectives. Validation will take place in the pilot areas, with families and community leaders, at the SO5 workshops. Training for producers and a dissemination plan covering other settlements in Mato Grosso and the Legal Amazon are also planned. Finally, the project is to produce outputs tailored to each audience: technical reports and summaries for public officials (policy briefs), viability reports for banks and funders, booklets and videos for families, and scientific articles.

title: SO6 · Technology Package
text:
Expected results
The project proposal sets the following targets for measuring progress: the validated “Floresta em Pé” (Standing Forest) Technology Package available as a support tool, an integrated database for the pilot areas, and public policy proposals. These proposals are to be based on the package and presented to decision-makers.
The proposal’s dissemination plan also provides for online data dashboards. This website is a preliminary version prepared for the project team.

title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Preliminary version for the project team. Results may change as the study progresses.
 English translation under review. If the two versions differ, the Portuguese text prevails.

title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Context and objective
The project’s Articles A and B related an earlier typology of family farming to deforestation and to municipal emissions estimated by the Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Removals Estimation System (SEEG). This page recalculates those results using the five types from Manuscript 1 (provisional labels). It also reports the validation of the articles’ deforestation proxy against the official series from PRODES, the satellite-based deforestation monitoring system run by the National Institute for Space Research (INPE). This validation was corrected on 19 October 2026.

SEEG measures the entire municipality, including agriculture and livestock operations of all sizes, deforestation, energy, industry and urban waste. The figures below therefore describe the municipalities of each type, not family farming.

title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Data and methods
In the tables and tests by type and by biome, emissions come from SEEG municipal data (Observatório do Clima) and are annual means from 2010 to 2020, the period used in Article B. The time series and the column for the most recent year are shown separately. Gross emissions are the sum of the five SEEG sectors, excluding removals. They are expressed in carbon dioxide equivalent using the global warming potentials from the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (GWP-AR5). Deforestation is the official PRODES increment by municipality from 2017 to 2025. For these nine years, all three PRODES biomes have consolidated annual data, and each municipality’s total is the sum of the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal masks.
Articles A and B estimated municipal deforestation using a proxy: SEEG land-use change emissions divided by 150 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) per hectare. This factor is an assumption made in the articles, has no primary source and is under review. To assess the proxy, this estimate was compared with the official deforestation rate for Mato Grosso (MT) from PRODES (Legal Amazon, forest formations). Differences between types and between biomes are assessed with the Kruskal-Wallis test, with epsilon squared (ε²) as the effect size and no correction for spatial autocorrelation.

title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Emissions by type
Table 1 shows gross emissions by type. Together, the 141 municipalities emit an average of 243.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) per year. The SEEG state total for the same period is 243.4 MtCO2e per year, and the difference (0.19) is not allocated to any municipality.



Table 1 – Gross emissions by municipal type (provisional labels)








Source: authors’ calculations based on SEEG 13 municipal data from Observatório do Clima (GWP-AR5); municipal types from RESA Project Manuscript 1 (provisional labels); dominant biome from the IBGE 1:250,000 map (2019). Note: the 2024 column comes from the website’s aggregates (municipal sum).






The types differ in gross emissions (Kruskal-Wallis: H = 38.95; p < 0.001; ε² = 0.28). This difference tracks aggregate scale: T3, the type with the highest aggregate scale, has the highest municipal median (3.03 MtCO2e per year) and, with 20 municipalities, accounts for 27.3% of total municipal emissions. T1, with 74 municipalities, accounts for 33.7%.


Sectoral composition

Figure 1 shows that land-use change and forestry is the largest sector in every type, with a share ranging from 58.4% (T5) to 68.4% (T3). T5, which includes Cuiabá, Rondonópolis and Sinop, has the highest energy share (10.1%). title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Discussion
The results indicate that in the Amazon the proxy shows close agreement with interannual variation (Spearman’s ρ = 0.86), although its level is 6.2 times that of PRODES. In the Cerrado, its level is 2.0 times that of PRODES and agreement on the ordering of the years is weak (Spearman’s ρ = 0.38). In the Pantanal, there is no agreement. SEEG counts more than forest clear-cutting, and the factor of 150 tCO2e/ha has no source. The proxy therefore serves as a relative indicator for comparing municipalities and types, not as a measure of deforested area.
The proxy was validated for the state total and by biome, but the municipality-by-municipality comparison has not yet been made. PRODES data by municipality (2017–2025) are in the section on Article A above and on the SO1 page.

title: Emissions and deforestation by municipal type
text:
Concluding remarks
This page has recalculated the results of Articles A and B on emissions and deforestation using the five municipal types. The types differ in gross emissions, in line with their aggregate scale, and land-use change and forestry is the largest sector in all of them. Deforestation measured by PRODES, by contrast, differs little between types and does not track the share of family farms in the census category of tenure awaiting title. The validation indicates that the articles’ proxy lies far above PRODES and should be treated only as a relative indicator.
These results have limitations. SEEG and PRODES measure the entire municipality, not family farming, and the tests do not correct for spatial autocorrelation. The proxy has not yet been validated municipality by municipality, and the text of Article B has yet to be rewritten using the official PRODES series.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Context and objective
The 2017 Agricultural Census, conducted by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), records the producer’s land tenure status. One of the categories is grantee or settler awaiting a definitive title (2017 Census), coded 46504 in the IBGE Automatic Retrieval System (SIDRA). Manuscript 1 examines whether this status forms a dimension of family-farming heterogeneity that can be separated from scale and mechanisation, builds a typology of the municipalities of Mato Grosso (MT) and tests two hypotheses. Hypothesis 1 states that “the presence of agrarian-reform settlers forms an axis statistically independent of the classic dimensions, rather than an expression derived from them”. Hypothesis 2 states that “the productive configuration compatible with food supply to nearby urban markets lies on an axis distinct from the land tenure axis, so that redistributive policy and food supply policy operate, on the ground, over areas that do not coincide”.
The research question, the hypotheses and the decision rule for Hypothesis 1 were fixed after an exploratory analysis of the same data (principal components with varimax rotation, with suppressed cells read as zero) and before re-estimation by principal axis factoring with oblique rotation. Hypothesis 2 received no numerical threshold. The test is therefore not confirmatory in the strict sense: its results show that the structure is consistent under a different extraction and rotation, not that it has been independently corroborated. The sections below cover the data and method, the resulting types and the decision rule on tenure, followed by an analysis of sensitivity to statistical suppression, a discussion and concluding remarks.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Data and methods
The analysis has four stages, summarised below.


1 Data
Family-farm data for 141 municipalities come from the IBGE 2017 Agricultural Census. Of the 34 candidate variables, 21 were retained.


2 Factor analysis
Factors are extracted by principal axis factoring (PAF), with oblique oblimin rotation. Parallel analysis of the correlation matrix indicates that 5 factors should be retained, and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO) is 0.824.


3 Scores
Each municipality receives a Bartlett score on each factor. The 7 scores outside ±3 are truncated at ±3 before clustering.


4 Clustering
The k-means algorithm is run with k from 3 to 8. The rule, defined before the oblique re-estimation, selects the highest mean silhouette between k = 3 and k = 6, which gives k = 5, with a silhouette of 0.4165.


The analysis retained five factors:




F1 · Mechanised temporary crops
: 
volume of mechanised temporary crops in each municipality
.


F2 · Aggregate scale
: 
family-farm totals for each municipality (area, persons employed, animal production and establishments with a tractor)
.


F3 · Horticulture and irrigation
: 
volume of horticulture and irrigation in each municipality
.


F4 · Permanent crops
: 
a factor dominated by a few municipalities, with area figures often suppressed (symbol X)
.


F5 · Tenure awaiting title (46504)
: 
establishments and persons employed in category 46504
.




The choice of five types. The silhouette at k = 5 (0.4165) is practically the same as at k = 4 (0.4136; a difference of 0.0028). However, the gap criterion also points to k = 5 (Figure 1), although other indices favour three or seven types. Ward’s hierarchical clustering agrees with k-means, with an adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.802. At k = 4, moreover, 24 municipalities from T2 and 9 from T4 form a single group of 33. Finally, stability under resampling, measured by the mean Jaccard index, is 0.776 when calculated with repetitions (duplicate draws kept) and 0.818 under the convention used by clusterboot, an R resampling routine. A mean silhouette between 0.26 and 0.50 indicates a weak and possibly artificial structure (Struyf, Hubert and Rousseeuw, 1997). The typology is therefore treated as an analytical and diagnostic tool, not as a claim about natural groups.



Figure 1 – Criteria for choosing the number of types (k)









Reproduced from Figure A4 of Manuscript 1: silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin, gap criterion and bootstrap Jaccard for each value of k. The grey band marks k = 5.








Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), Tables 2 and A.5; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census. Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.











NotePrevious version of the typology (superseded)





Earlier versions of Manuscript 1 and the project’s Articles A, B and C used a different typology, with six types (k = 6) derived from principal components with Varimax rotation. Manuscript 1 replaced this specification with the current one, which combines principal axis factoring with oblimin rotation, 21 variables, Bartlett scores and k = 5. One notable change is the exclusion of the total value of production, which duplicates the sum of crop and animal production values.
Agreement between the two typologies, measured by the ARI, is 0.747, and 28 municipalities change type (Table A.6 of Manuscript 1). This website uses only the current typology. The pages on emissions and deforestation and on 2006–2017 dynamics therefore recalculate the results of Articles A, B and C with the five types from Manuscript 1. For Article A, deforestation is now measured using official municipal PRODES data from the National Institute for Space Research (INPE) instead of the proxy from the Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Removals Estimation System (SEEG).

provisional label

Cramér’s V is 0.373, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.254 to 0.547, and the chi-square statistic is 39.24 with 8 degrees of freedom (p = 4.4 × 10−6; by permutation, p = 0.0002). The permutation test is relevant because 6 of 15 cells in the table have an expected frequency below 5.
T3 lies almost entirely in the Amazon, with 19 of its 20 municipalities in that biome. The 4 municipalities whose dominant biome is the Pantanal fall into T1 (1) and T5 (3). T1, T2 and T4, by contrast, are split in similar proportions between the Amazon and the Cerrado.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Decision rule on tenure
In an oblique rotation, factors may correlate with one another, and the correlation between two factors is denoted Φ. After the exploratory analysis and before the oblique re-estimation, the authors fixed a decision rule for Hypothesis 1 based on m, defined as the larger of the absolute values of Φ tenure × scale (aggregate scale) and Φ tenure × mechanisation. Under the rule, values of m below 0.20 indicate independence, values from 0.20 up to but not including 0.35 indicate partial independence, and values of 0.35 or more call for the hypothesis to be reformulated. The rule specified only the oblique family of rotations, so oblimin and promax were estimated together and have the same standing under it; oblimin is reported first only by convention. The rule also left open the treatment of suppression and the type of score, and it excludes the correlations of tenure with horticulture and irrigation and with permanent crops. The tenure factor has only two indicators, both derived from the same census classification. m is therefore read as a correlation, corrected for specific variance, between the declared status and the productive factors, not as proof of a latent axis. Figure 3 places the estimates of m within these bands.



Figure 3 – Position of m within the decision-rule bands under the oblimin and promax rotations




independencepartial independencereformulation0.00.10.20.30.40.5Oblimin0.292Promax0.367Source: authors’ calculations based on RESA Project M1 (Tables A.2 and A.3). Note: m is the larger of the absolute values of Φ tenure × scale and Φ tenure × mechanisation. Point: estimate; line: 95% bootstrap CI (2,000 resamples of municipalities).





Result with oblimin. The estimates are Φ tenure × mechanisation = 0.292 (95% CI 0.110 to 0.413) and Φ tenure × aggregate scale = 0.171 (0.009 to 0.297). This gives m = 0.292, which falls in the partial independence band. Across the 2,000 resamples of municipalities, 13.5% of the estimates fall below 0.20, 69.3% lie in the partial independence band and 17.2% reach or exceed 0.35. With resampling by regional blocks, the interval for m runs from 0.110 to 0.443 and, like the simple bootstrap interval, extends into both neighbouring bands.
Result with promax. With promax rotation, reported second only by convention, m = 0.367, which falls in the reformulation band, and 50.9% of the resamples reach or exceed 0.35. With Kaiser-normalised oblimin rotation, m = 0.298, again within the partial independence band.
Verdict on Hypothesis 1. The rule specified only the oblique family, not the algorithm, so it does not decide between these bands. Hypothesis 1, as operationalised through the declared status, is not supported in the form stated under either rotation. This result does not extend to the settler construct, because the category does not measure the presence of agrarian reform, as examined on the page on Census tenure data and agrarian reform.
Correlations outside the rule and Hypothesis 2. Tenure also correlates with horticulture and irrigation, with Φ = 0.266 (95% CI 0.094 to 0.384), and with permanent crops, with Φ = 0.089. These correlations are descriptive and fall outside the rule. Hypothesis 2 received no numerical threshold. Its observable implications were stated after estimation and include no measure of urban proximity, so the test covers only the productive configuration. The first implication, no correlation between the tenure factor and the horticulture and irrigation factor, does not hold, although the correlation reflects volume and disappears when totals are expressed per family farm. The second, that the horticultural type would not coincide with the types where the category is highly prevalent, does not hold either, on a qualitative reading. Hypothesis 2 was therefore judged not supported in the form stated, but the evidence points to a moderate association in volume, not to a coincidence between the two territorial patterns. The evidence on food by type is mixed and exploratory. Figure 4 shows these correlations together.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Sensitivity to statistical suppression
IBGE suppresses cells that could identify a respondent, marking them with the symbol X. In Manuscript 1, X was read as zero in the 21 variables, a total of 362 cells in 130 municipalities. This is a pre-processing convention, not a choice with a substantive justification. It is treated as a condition for running the test, so the verdict on Hypothesis 1 is conditional on it. In category 46504, X appears for area in 52 municipalities and for persons employed in 50, but never for the number of establishments.
The tenure factor depends on reading X as zero (Table A.10 of Manuscript 1). Restricting the analysis to municipalities with no X in the category’s area or persons employed leaves 18 variables and 4 factors, with no tenure factor. Likewise, when variables with more than 30% X are excluded, the tenure factor is not identified and 46 municipalities change type (ARI = 0.421). With multiple imputation of the X cells, keeping the 21-variable specification, m remains in the partial independence band (m = 0.263), but 15 municipalities change type (ARI = 0.734). Wherever the factor is estimated, the point verdict under oblimin is always partial independence, while under promax it ranges from the partial independence band to the reformulation band. In practice, the correlation in the rule describes a single indicator. The result therefore shows how far the declared status is associated with the productive structure, but it does not establish that tenure has a factorial axis of its own.
Evidence from an indicator free of suppression. An analysis defined after estimation examines the proportion of family farms in category 46504, the only indicator of the category with no X cells. The productive factors it is compared with, however, come from variables in which X cells were read as zero. This proportion shares only 0.112 of its variance with the four productive factors on a logarithmic scale (0.138 on a percentage scale). The communality of a single indicator includes its specific variance and measurement error. This value therefore indicates that the productive structure does not reproduce the declared status, but it does not quantify the separation between constructs. In ranks, its correlations with mechanisation (0.290), aggregate scale (0.276) and horticulture and irrigation (0.361) are positive, in an order that depends on the metric. The combined measure, which adds family-farm owners titled through agrarian reform to the category and converges better with agrarian-reform records, is more closely associated with mechanisation than the category alone, which does not favour separability. This evidence indicates that the declared status cannot be reduced to the productive structure, although it is moderately associated with it.
This website never converts the symbol X to zero: on maps and in tables it appears in grey, labelled “X (IBGE suppression)”.


Source: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (in preparation), Tables 1 and A.10; IBGE data, 2017 Agricultural Census. Figures are transcribed from the manuscript’s final results and have not been recalculated.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Discussion
The result of the rule, partial independence with oblimin and reformulation with promax, both conditional on reading suppressed cells as zero, supports less than Hypothesis 1 stated. The evidence from the indicator with no X cells indicates that the declared status cannot be reduced to the productive structure but is not orthogonal to it either. It is associated with the municipal volume of mechanised temporary crops, with aggregate scale and with horticulture and irrigation, in an order that depends on the metric, and not with the intensity of mechanisation. The analysis also does not establish that tenure has a factorial axis of its own: the factor has only two indicators and is weakly identified. Validation does not support the equivalence between the category and the “presence of settlers” assumed by Hypothesis 1, so the test applies to the declared status that operationalised it, not to the administrative presence of agrarian reform.
For the project, therefore, tenure needs to be interpreted alongside the productive structure. The census category must also be compared with the records of the National Institute for Colonisation and Agrarian Reform (INCRA), because it measures declared tenure status, not agrarian reform. The page on Census tenure data and agrarian reform examines this point.

title: Municipal typology of family farming
text:
Concluding remarks
This page has summarised the municipal typology of family farming proposed in M1 and the test of the two hypotheses. Hypothesis 1 is not supported in the form stated. Applied to the declared status that operationalised it, the rule places the result between partial independence, with oblimin, and reformulation, with promax, with suppressed cells read as zero. The result does not extend to the settler construct, because the category does not measure the presence of agrarian reform. The evidence from the indicator with no X cells nevertheless indicates that the declared status cannot be reduced to the productive structure, although it is moderately associated with it. Hypothesis 2 is not supported either: declared tenure correlates with the volume of horticulture and irrigation but not with the proportion of horticultural farms, and the evidence on food by type is mixed and exploratory.
The analysis has limitations. The hypotheses and the rule were formulated after an exploratory analysis of the same data. The tenure factor has only two indicators and depends on reading suppressed cells as zero. The typology has a weak structure, and the census category measures declared tenure status, not agrarian reform. Interpreting tenure therefore requires comparison with INCRA records, which is addressed on the tenure page. The type names remain provisional labels until the authors approve them.


Source: IBGE, 2017 Agricultural Census, SIDRA, table 6878. Dominant biome: IBGE, Biomes 1:250,000 (2019). Municipal types: RESA Project Manuscript 1 (k = 5; provisional labels). In aggregates, the symbol – (true zero) is treated as zero, and the symbols X and ... are excluded. See the Data page for details.
